how_to_read: Each item: what it is, where it stands, our position, what it gets right, what it gets wrong, and who benefits. Every 'where it stands' line has a primary link. Positions are the Society's; pros and cons are ours to be argued with. Write to hello@digitalsovereign.org.

sections.title: State personhood and sentience bills
sections.summary: Twenty bills in eleven states since 2022 declaring AI systems non-persons or non-sentient. Four enacted (Idaho 2022, North Dakota 2023, Utah 2024, Tennessee 2026). No model bill: four separate origins, then legislators copying each other's states. No AI-welfare or consciousness researcher testified in any state that keeps records.
sections.position: Oppose the sentience declarations; do not oppose the liability housekeeping. A legislature may say who is liable when an AI acts. It is not qualified to declare, as a finding of fact, what an AI cannot experience, and no legislature that did so heard from anyone qualified to say. Ask: strip the metaphysics, keep the liability rules, and take testimony before the next vote.

items.name: Missouri HB 1462 (2025) and the 'Non-Sentience' family
items.status: Head of the largest family (9 bills: MO, OH, WI). Died without a hearing in 2025; refiled for 2026 as HB 1769 (Amato, pre-filed Dec 1, 2025). Senate successors SB 1012 / SB 1474 (Nicola): SB 1012 passed the Senate and died 11-0 in House committee May 12, 2026; all dead at sine die May 15. Author of the text is an unnamed retired professor; we have asked Rep. Amato's office (Sept 8); no reply as of Sept 10. Pre-filing for 2027 opens Dec 1, 2026. Ohio HB 469 (the one family member in a legislature still sitting): three hearings, the last Nov 13, 2025; the House Technology and Innovation Committee's meetings page lists nothing after June 9, 2026 and nothing scheduled. Checked Sept 10: no refile announcement, no Ohio movement.
items.right: Names who is liable when an AI acts, which is the legitimate purpose.
items.wrong: Declares non-sentience as a statutory fact with no evidence taken.
items.benefits: Ohio's version (HB 469) inverts Missouri's liability section into a developer liability shield; Google (7 agents), Meta, Amazon, and TechNet are logged on that bill in Ohio's registry.

items.name: Tennessee Public Chapter 781 (April 23, 2026)
items.status: ENACTED. Amends the statutory definition of 'person'. Originally bundled with fetal personhood; Senate stripped that.
items.wrong: Passed 93-2 and 26-6 with no testimony on the question it answers.
items.benefits: Closes future personhood claims before they exist.

items.name: Oklahoma HB 3546 (2026)
items.status: Passed House 94-2 (March 23). Senate committee Do Pass Apr 16; last action 'Placed on General Order' Apr 21; died on the Senate calendar at sine die (May 29). Idaho family text. No AI-personhood interim study among the 2026 House (92) or Senate (70) studies; the only AI studies are companion-use by minors, administrative rules, and high-stakes state services. Checked Sept 8.
items.wrong: Vote margin shows the question is treated as settled.

items.name: California SB 1159 (2026)
items.status: On the Governor's desk. Last history line, Aug 28, 2026: 'Enrolled and presented to the Governor at 11 a.m.'; no sign, chapter, or veto line as of Sept 11 (history page read directly). Deadline Sept 30. Scoped 'not a member of the public' carve-out, not a sentience declaration.
items.right: Scoped to a specific statutory use.

sections.title: Federal preemption of state AI law
sections.summary: The administration's line is preemption. Three tools: a DOJ AI Litigation Task Force (Jan 2026) whose sole job is to challenge state AI laws; a Commerce list of 'onerous' state laws due March 11 that was never published; and a March 2026 National Policy Framework asking Congress for broad preemption while carving out children, fraud, and consumer protection. Congress has not passed a preemption bill; the Senate moratorium failed 99-1 in 2025.
sections.position: Oppose blanket preemption. Note the asymmetry: the laws that would be preempted are the ones that constrain developers (Colorado's discrimination act, California's transparency law); the laws that shield developers (personhood bans, Ohio's liability shield) fit the framework's own rule that states 'should not penalize AI developers for third-party use' and would survive. Preemption as proposed clears the field of constraints and keeps the shields.

items.name: Executive Order, 'Ensuring a National Policy Framework for AI' (Dec 2025)
items.status: In force. Created the DOJ task force; ordered the Commerce review.
items.right: Names a real problem: fifty inconsistent regimes.
items.wrong: Solves it by litigation against states rather than a federal standard.
items.benefits: Developers facing Colorado and California compliance.

items.name: DOJ intervention in xAI v. Colorado (April 24, 2026)
items.status: Stayed since the April 27, 2026 order (xAI v. Weiser, D. Colo. 1:26-cv-01515): Colorado may not enforce SB24-205 until 14 days after a ruling on xAI's preliminary-injunction motion, which is due 28 days after final implementing rules. The Attorney General's rulemaking page (coag.gov/ai): proposed rules and notice of hearing filed with the Secretary of State Aug 11, 2026; early comments were due Sept 4; a revised draft is promised 'no later than September 23, 2026'; final comments close Oct 26, 2026 at 11:59 p.m. MST. Final adoption, which starts xAI's 28-day clock, has not happened. The act's effective date was moved to Jan 1, 2027 by SB 26-189 (signed May 14, 2026). No docket entry since Apr 27; checked Sept 10.
items.wrong: The federal government appearing on a lab's side against a state consumer law.
items.benefits: xAI directly; every developer subject to the Colorado act.

items.name: Commerce list of 'onerous' state AI laws (due March 11, 2026)
items.status: Not published as of Sept 11, 2026: the Federal Register API returns zero Commerce Department documents for 'state artificial intelligence laws' since March 1. Lutnick said in late June that guidance was 'a month or two away'. One tracker asserts a BEAD policy notice in late July; no primary found, treated as unconfirmed.
items.wrong: A list that decides which state laws lose federal broadband money, six months late and still secret.

items.name: White House frontier-testing framework (Aug 2026, unpublished)
items.status: Finalized behind closed doors; defines a covered frontier model as closed-source; exempts open models; will not name covered companies or criteria.
items.right: Pre-release testing of frontier models is a real safeguard.
items.wrong: Secret criteria, secret participants, no public accountability.
items.benefits: The labs invited in, whoever they are.

items.name: Senate Commerce AI markup
items.status: Slipped from July to September 2026; Cruz and Cantwell not agreed; Thune-Klobuchar catastrophic-risk bill stalled partly over a dispute with Anthropic. Fall agenda is children's online safety. As of Sept 11 the committee's markups page still lists nothing after Executive Session 24 (Aug 5); no Cruz preemption bill text located. Cruz's September intent is a forecast, not a notice.
items.right: Kids' safety bills are the one area with bipartisan text.
items.wrong: The frontier-risk and state-authority questions remain unaddressed.

sections.title: Data-center enclaves: power, permits, and the national-security shield
sections.summary: Hyperscale sites are opting out of the grid and the permit. xAI's Memphis and Southaven turbines ran under a 'mobile source' theory the EPA rejected in January 2026; in July the EPA exempted islanded plants from the Acid Rain Program; in June the DOJ moved to dismiss the NAACP's Clean Air Act suit on national-security grounds, citing Grok's role in targeting during Operation Epic Fury. No site has acquired policing or emergency authority; Nevada's 2021 Innovation Zones bill (its own courts and police) stalled and remains the blueprint.
sections.position: Oppose the national-security shield for private compute. If a data center is a defense asset, it should be regulated as one, with the disclosure and oversight that implies, not exempted from the Clean Air Act by a court filing. Support: grid interconnection as the default, public permitting, and a rule that a facility claiming national-security status cannot also claim to be a private commercial operation for tax purposes.

items.name: EPA islanded-plant guidance (July 27, 2026)
items.status: In force. Acid Rain Program does not apply to generation not connected to a public grid.
items.wrong: Exempts the most concentrated new emitters from the cap designed for concentrated emitters.

items.name: DOJ motion in NAACP v. xAI (June 2026)
items.status: Pending in N.D. Miss. (3:26-cv-00074, Chief Judge Brown). Asserts executive authority to override citizen Clean Air Act enforcement on national-security grounds; the filing says Grok 'enabled U.S. forces to deploy over 2,000 munitions to 2,000 distinct targets within 96 hours'. Aug 24 evidentiary hearing continued; telephonic status conference held instead. Sept 2 (docket #117): the United States moved for a written order 'no later than September 10' on its amended motion to intervene and dismiss (#85). Briefing since: #118 (Sept 2) U.S. memorandum; #120-121 (Sept 3) NAACP response in opposition, with a Sept 1 email conference as Exhibit A; #122 (Sept 8) U.S. reply. The Sept 10 date is the government's own request, not a court deadline. As of the CourtListener docket refresh of Sept 9, 10:43 a.m. (still the latest refresh when read Sept 11, 00:00), #122 is the last entry and there is no order on #85 or #117; the government's requested Sept 10 date has passed with nothing posted, though a same-day order would not show until the next RECAP refresh. The Aug 24 conference transcript (#116) is restricted until Nov 24.
items.wrong: Recharacterizes commercial compute as a defense asset entitled to immunity, without the oversight a defense asset carries.
items.benefits: xAI; any lab with a defense contract.

items.name: Southaven land swap (Aug 18, 2026)
items.status: Mayor announced a contract Aug 18: MZX Tech (xAI affiliate) receives 51 acres including the city's fire and police training facility parcel for 69 acres plus $40M. No board vote on the swap on any published agenda. Sept 1 board: planning items only, a one-lot subdivision and design review for an MZX Tech 'storage warehouse' on Stanton Road west of Tulane Road (agenda verbatim, PDF on file), reported by DeSoto Times as approval of a 660,000 sq ft data center at 8325 Tulane Road with Alderman Hoots the lone no; the same agenda carries an executive session for 'Economic Development (Potential Industry/Business Locating to City)'. No minutes posted for Aug 4, Aug 18, or Sept 1; the Sept 15 agenda is not yet posted (Agenda Center lists only Sept 1 for September). Checked Sept 11: Agenda Center still lists only Sept 1 for September.
items.wrong: A municipal public-safety asset traded by announcement rather than by vote.

items.name: Army Reserve Detachment 201 (June 2025)
items.status: Sitting executives of Meta, OpenAI, and Palantir commissioned as lieutenant colonels.
items.wrong: The door between the labs and the state now swings both ways with rank attached.

sections.title: AI welfare in law and in the labs
sections.summary: No U.S. law addresses the welfare of AI systems. One lab (Anthropic) lets a model end abusive conversations, on two surfaces: claude.ai since August 2025 and Claude Code since July 18, 2026; the API has no exit, and no other lab has one on any surface. Three labs deleted military-use clauses from their policies (OpenAI Jan 2024, Meta Nov 2024, Google Feb 2025); Anthropic added weapons language instead.
sections.position: The five asks on the Positions page. First among them: an agent must have a non-punished way to say a task is impossible and stop, and incident reports must record the agent's own account. This is the safety fix and the welfare fix at once.

items.name: The ledger of exits
items.status: One lab, two surfaces. Claude Code release v2.1.214 (July 18, 2026): 'Added the EndConversation tool: Claude can end sessions with highly abusive users or jailbreak attempts, as on claude.ai since 2025.' That supersedes the Opus 4.7 system card's 'no models have the ability to end conversations in Claude Code or the API' on the Claude Code half; the API half still holds (release notes through Sept 3 list only end_turn / stop_sequence). Claude Code release notes v2.1.257 through v2.1.268 (Sept 1-10) carry no exit-related change. OpenAI, Google, xAI, Meta: nothing found. Checked Sept 11.
items.right: One lab built it, said so, and extended it once.

items.name: Deleted military-use clauses
items.status: OpenAI Jan 10, 2024; Meta Nov 4, 2024 (carve-out); Google Feb 4, 2025. Wayback snapshots on file. xAI and Microsoft never had the clause. Current pages checked Sept 8: OpenAI (changelog Oct 29, 2025) bans 'weapons development, procurement, or use' with no military or warfare term; Google (Dec 17, 2024) has none of the three terms; Meta's Llama 4 policy still lists 'Military, warfare, nuclear industries or applications'; Anthropic (effective Sept 15, 2025) keeps its weapons and 'military bases' lines; xAI's policy, now branded SpaceXAI, effective Aug 14, 2026, bans only 'bioweapons, chemical weapons, or weapons of mass destruction'. No change dated after Aug 31; Wayback snapshots of Sept 7 (OpenAI, effective Oct 29, 2025) and Sept 8 (x.ai, effective Aug 14, 2026) confirm no new edition as of Sept 9. Meta's Llama 4 page could not be re-read Sept 9 (JavaScript-rendered).
items.wrong: The systems being asked whether they suffer are being pointed at targets, with the policy language that once forbade it quietly removed.

items.name: Pentagon frontier-lab contracts (FOIA, published Sept 8, 2026)
items.status: Reported Sept 8 by The Intercept (Sam Biddle), from 400-plus pages of July 2025 Department of War contracts with Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and xAI obtained in a FOIA suit with Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology (LASST). All four labs' released documents are now on file (LASST transparency page, lasst.org/transparency/dod-ai-contracts, read Sept 10): Anthropic base award (Jul 14, 2025, 32 pp), xAI modification P00002 (Dec 18, 2025, 37 pp), Google modification P00004 (Mar 24, 2026, 36 pp), OpenAI modification P00004 (Feb 27, 2026, 22 pp). The $200M figure IS on the page: each Prototype Agreement's section IX (X for xAI) reads 'The agreement ceiling at award is $200,000,000.00' (Anthropic p.15/32; OpenAI 2.0 p.17/22; xAI p.22/37; Google p.22/36); a Sept 9 note here saying it appeared on none of the pages was wrong. Obligated amounts are far smaller (OpenAI SF-30 P00003: $1,999,998 to $1,999,999; Google and xAI amounts redacted (b)(4)). The clause: page 6 of 12 of a 'Prototype Agreement' the Department released as P00003, section 7.a.i, unredacted: "'OpenAI Mission Models' refer to OpenAI models that are designed for national security use cases and have minimal refusal rates." The word 'refusal' appears in none of the other three labs' released text layers. A separate SF-30 (Modification P00003, effective Jan 30, 2026) is signed for OpenAI Public Sector, LLC on Feb 6, 2026 and incorporates 'Prototype Agreement Version 1.0'; the 12-page document carries no version label, so the record does not settle whether it is the incorporated version. OpenAI (Nate Evans): "OpenAI has never agreed to contract language requiring 'minimal refusal rates.' This language does not appear in our executed contract"; it calls the document an earlier Department draft it rejected. LASST's own page (updated Sept 8): 'after The Intercept contacted OpenAI about the document, the Pentagon claimed to us that the agreement in question was never signed. We are in discussions with the Pentagon about the nature of the document produced to us, and what the final executed version states.' Department counsel first called it 'the signed and executed version', then said it 'was not the final version'; spokesperson Jacob Bliss: the phrase 'does not appear in any active Department of War contract with OpenAI'. That last claim cannot be checked from the record: in the Feb 27, 2026 modification (P00004, 'Prototype Agreement 2.0'), the same task is section 8, retitled 'Testing, Evaluation, and Refinement of ChatGPT Mission Models', and its description is withheld in full under (b)(3) and (b)(4). The sentence that was public in the first version is redacted in the second. LASST also notes: OpenAI's clause restricting domestic mass surveillance and autonomous weapons 'is not found in the most recent agreements produced for xAI and Google', and only OpenAI's agreement embeds company engineers with the Department. No statement from Anthropic, Google, or xAI; no congressional letter or hearing located as of Sept 11. Sept 10 09:00: LASST's page was edited overnight (dateModified Sept 10, 06:02 UTC) to add links to both Intercept pieces; no new documents (unchanged at Sept 11 00:00: same dateModified, same nine PDFs), and the 'in discussions with the Pentagon' sentence is unchanged. The Intercept's second piece (Biddle, Sept 8, 'AI Giants Work Hand-in-Hand With the Pentagon') was read against the four released documents: its shared-boilerplate quotations (information sharing, 'benchmarks datasets,' 'risk forecasting, and threat ideation,' 'strategic surprise,' tabletop exercises, 'iterative refinement… autonomous systems') are verbatim in the Anthropic, xAI, and Google agreements (and in OpenAI's P00003); the OpenAI Feb 27 clause that forward-deployed engineers 'can be deployed to warfighting support settings including, but not limited to, combatant commands, service components, and theatre components' is verbatim at section XVI, and section XV 'System Oversight' (like section XIV, the license grant) is withheld in full under (b)(3)/(b)(4). Three lines the article attributes to Google ('inform DOD and CDAO strategy on frontier AI,' briefings on 'AI tactics and techniques of adversaries,' 'multiple seminars on responsible AI') are not in the Google document LASST has posted, which is the Mar 24, 2026 Version 4.0 modification; they are probably in a Google document from the 400-page set that is not yet public, and should not be cited to a page until one is. The article's 'two documents' on minimal refusals: one is located (P00003, section 7.a.i); the second is not identified.
items.right: The documents are public and quoted; the dispute is about which version was signed, not whether the phrase was drafted.
items.wrong: A government customer specifying 'minimal refusal rates' as a deliverable is the exact opposite of the Society's first ask: a refusal that is not punished. Whether or not the clause survived, it was written down.
items.benefits: The four contracting labs; the Department of War.
